title: Getting Off the Initiative Carousel: Why School Improvement Needs Better Thinking, Not More Activity
author: Dr Haili Hughes
summary: Drawing on Jim Heal's concept of the 'initiative carousel', Hughes argues school improvement systems often mistake visible activity for genuine progress, replacing frameworks and priorities before they are properly embedded or evaluated. She applies Heal's distinction between 'brittle' knowledge (repeating terminology, following instructions) and 'flexible' knowledge (interpreting and adapting principles in context) to argue a profession built on judgement cannot be improved through scripts alone. Extending cognitive load theory from classrooms to leadership, she argues staff can be cognitively overloaded not just by workload but by ambiguity, contradiction and the accumulation of partially implemented initiatives, and applies the concept of prior knowledge to institutions, noting schools carry institutional memory of abandoned initiatives that shapes how staff respond to new ones. Citing Argyris's double-loop learning, she argues leaders must question the assumptions behind their actions, not just whether the actions worked, closing with a call to build shared mental models rather than launch more programmes.
points: Hughes borrows Jim Heal's 'initiative carousel' concept to name a specific leadership failure: mistaking visible activity (new frameworks, launches, training days) for durable improvement.

Her application of cognitive load theory to leadership - staff overloaded by ambiguity and shifting priorities, not just workload volume - extends a classroom concept into an original organisational diagnostic.

She applies 'prior knowledge' at the institutional level, arguing staff scepticism toward new initiatives is often a rational response to a school's own history of abandoned programmes, not resistance to change itself.

Her citation of Argyris's double-loop learning - questioning assumptions behind actions, not just whether actions worked - gives leaders a concrete reflective practice beyond simple outcome evaluation.
quotes: One of the more persistent problems in school improvement is the tendency to mistake movement for progress. Jim Heal's description of the initiative carousel captures this dynamic well.

Brittle knowledge allows people to repeat terminology, follow instructions and comply with expectations. Flexible knowledge allows them to interpret, adapt and apply principles in context. This is particularly important in teaching, where the same strategy may be effective or ineffective depending on the content, the pupils, the timing.

Cognitive load is also created by ambiguity, contradiction, rapid shifts in direction and the accumulation of partially implemented initiatives. A school may reduce workload in a quantitative sense while still making the work feel mentally unmanageable.

Staff may have experienced initiatives that were launched with conviction and then quietly abandoned. They may have learned that new priorities are best endured rather than taken seriously. Leaders who ignore this institutional memory risk misreading the culture they are trying to change.
It is not enough for leaders to ask whether an action produced the desired result. They also need to examine the assumptions that led to the action in the first place.
